recipe.history:
The blank canvas — the unmarked page, the empty pan, the unnamed dish — has a philosophy behind it that is as old as cooking itself. Every culinary tradition carries within it a category of food that is defined not by a single dominant ingredient but by the harmonious assembly of many quiet ones, each contributing its measure without claiming the spotlight. The compound herb butter is one of the oldest such preparations in the European kitchen: a simple technology of incorporating aromatics into fat that dates at least to medieval French cuisine, where butter was enriched with herbs, spices, and sometimes wine before being applied to roasted meats. The practice requires nothing exotic — only quality butter, fresh herbs, and the patience to let the fat absorb the aromatics over time — and the result is a condiment of remarkable versatility and depth. Aged Gouda, meanwhile, represents the Dutch tradition of long-ripened cow's milk cheese, a tradition that reaches back centuries to the farmhouses and canal-side markets of South Holland, where wheels were aged on wooden boards until the interior crystallized into dense, caramel-sweet, deeply complex paste.

The toasted sesame bun is an American invention that took an Asian ingredient — the sesame seed, cultivated in sub-Saharan Africa and the Indus Valley for at least three thousand years and one of the first crops traded along ancient maritime routes — and made it the defining texture and flavor marker of the standard American hamburger bun. The seeds toast as the bun bakes, releasing their nutty oil, adding a crunch to the crust that is now so deeply associated with the idea of a burger that its absence is immediately noticed. Mixed greens — the combination of delicate lettuces, peppery arugula, and tender herbs — became the default salad base of American restaurant culture in the 1980s and 1990s, a development driven partly by California cuisine's valorization of fresh, lightly dressed greens as both a health statement and an aesthetic choice. Together, these four elements — herb butter, aged Gouda, mixed greens, sesame bun — compose a burger that is complete without being complicated, a blank canvas that becomes a self-portrait.

I have made this burger more times than I can count, often on evenings when I have no plan and no particular inspiration, when I open the refrigerator and find butter and herbs and a wedge of good cheese. There is something profoundly reassuring about a burger that asks nothing more of you than your full attention — no exotic ingredients, no complicated techniques, only the care to make each element as good as it can be. The herb butter teaches you to pay attention to the herbs in your garden or your windowsill pot. The aged Gouda teaches you to appreciate cheese that has been allowed to become something more than it started as. The mixed greens teach you that freshness is a quality that deteriorates in direct proportion to neglect. And the sesame bun teaches you that even the most familiar things deserve to be made well.

Cooking a blank canvas burger to medium rare is not a philosophy of the dramatic or the extraordinary — it is a philosophy of the everyday done correctly. At 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, the patty is an ordinary miracle: ground beef that has been transformed by heat into something with crust and juice and the specific internal softness of properly cooked muscle. The herb butter melting on the surface of this patty is the finishing argument. It asks the question — is there a reason to cook this further, to drive out the juice and flatten the flavor and turn the rose center grey? — and the answer is always no. There is never a reason. Medium rare is the answer to the blank canvas. It is the only color you need.
ingredients: 1 egg beaten with 1 tbsp water (egg wash)
3 tbsp sesame seeds (mix of white and black if available)
1 tbsp fresh flat-leaf parsley, finely chopped
1 tsp fresh rosemary, very finely minced
1 small clove garlic, minced to a paste
80g mixed baby greens (arugula, spinach, frisée, mâche)
4 slices aged Gouda (at least 18 months old)
instructions: 1. Make the compound herb butter: Combine softened butter, parsley, chives, thyme, rosemary, garlic paste, lemon zest, salt, and pepper in a bowl and mix until thoroughly combined. Roll onto a sheet of plastic wrap, form into a log about 1.5 inches in diameter, twist the ends tight, and refrigerate for at least 2 hours. Can be made up to 1 week ahead.

2. Make the bun dough: Combine warm milk, yeast, and sugar in the bowl of a stand mixer and let sit 5 minutes until foamy. Add flour, salt, butter, and egg. Mix on medium with the dough hook for 8–10 minutes until smooth and elastic.
3. Transfer to a lightly oiled bowl, cover, and let rise until doubled, about 1 to 1.5 hours.

4. Divide dough into 4 equal portions (about 150g each). Shape each into a tight smooth ball. Place on a parchment-lined baking sheet spacing at least 3 inches apart. Cover loosely and let rise until puffy and doubled, about 45 minutes.

5. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Brush buns generously with egg wash. Sprinkle liberally with sesame seeds, pressing them gently to adhere. Bake 16–18 minutes until deep golden brown. Cool on a wire rack.
6. Make the vinaigrette: Whisk together olive oil, white wine vinegar, Dijon mustard, salt, and pepper in a small bowl until emulsified. Set aside.

7. Prepare the patties: Divide ground beef into 4 portions of about 170g each. Form gently into patties about 3/4 inch thick with a thumb dimple in the center. Season both sides with salt and pepper. Refrigerate 15 minutes.
8. Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Cook patties 3 minutes first side without pressing. Flip and cook 2–3 minutes second side.
9. Lay a slice of aged Gouda on each patty. Add a splash of water, cover immediately, and steam 30–45 seconds until the cheese is melted and pooling at the edges.

10. Transfer patties to a resting rack. Slice two rounds of compound herb butter (about 1/4 inch thick) and lay on top of each hot patty. Rest 3–4 minutes. Target internal temperature is 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. The butter will melt into the meat as it rests.
11. Toss mixed greens with vinaigrette just before assembly.
12. Split and toast buns cut-side down in a dry skillet over medium heat until golden, about 1–2 minutes.

13. Assemble: Spread mayonnaise on the bottom bun and whole grain mustard on the top bun. Place sliced tomatoes on the bottom bun. Set the patty with melted compound butter and Gouda on the tomatoes. Add a few thin shallot rings. Pile dressed mixed greens on top. Finish with flaky sea salt. Set the top bun in place and serve immediately.
